key_finding: NIS-Agent's context isolation at webpage triage and answer validation reduces inertia bias, cutting token cost by 33% while matching baseline performance on GAIA, WebWalkerQA, BrowseComp and BrowseComp-zh.
methodology: Introduces the IBIS benchmark to isolate inertia bias, then evaluates NIS-Agent (context isolation at two decision points) plus a fine-tuned 8B model across four deep-research benchmarks.
why_it_matters: Identifies a specific failure mode (self-authored action history distorting judgment) and a specific corrective mechanism (context isolation), giving a concrete candidate for attributing agentic gains rather than crediting the system as a whole.
limitations: Evaluated on general web/QA benchmarks (GAIA, BrowseComp), not scientific literature search specifically
no comparison to a single-query database baseline
relevance_reason: Isolates a specific agentic failure mode and mechanism, relevant to decision 2 on what agentic moves carry the gain.

key_finding: Search effort and answer quality are only weakly aligned; answer accuracy correlates more with cumulative retrieval recall than with number of searches, and useful evidence often appears early while agents keep searching redundantly.
methodology: Trajectory-level diagnosis of six long-horizon search agents on BrowseComp-Plus (fixed retrieval, human-annotated document-level relevance judgments), validated on BrowseComp with an open-web API; decomposes failures into retrieval gaps vs. utilization gaps.
why_it_matters: Directly undercuts the premise that more iterative agentic search reliably improves outcomes, showing that the best agents issue fewer redundant queries — this reframes what an 'agentic gain' should be measured against and how stopping criteria should be designed.
limitations: Limited to six agents and two benchmarks (BrowseComp-Plus, BrowseComp)
retrieval model and harness held fixed, so findings may not generalize to other retrievers
relevance_reason: Directly answers decision 4 (where reported gains fail to hold) by showing search effort doesn't track answer quality, using controlled relevance judgments relevant to decision 3 as well.

key_finding: Even leading deep-research agents (Gemini DR, OpenAI DR) achieve under 68% average compliance with 2,500+ expert-written rubrics across domain-diverse prompts.
methodology: ResearchRubrics benchmark built with 2,800+ hours of human labor pairing realistic prompts with fine-grained expert rubrics, plus a three-axis complexity taxonomy and human/model-based evaluation protocols.
why_it_matters: A rigorously constructed rubric-based benchmark showing current deep-research agents fall well short of full compliance, directly informing how evaluation sets should be built and interpreted (decision 3) rather than trusting self-reported end-to-end scores.
limitations: Rubric-based scoring does not directly measure recall against a single-query baseline
domain-diverse prompts may not map cleanly onto scientific literature search specifically
relevance_reason: A rigorously constructed benchmark with explicit labeling methodology — central evidence for how evaluation sets for literature-search-like agents should be built.

key_finding: On a fixed, curated corpus, Search-R1 with BM25 achieves only 3.86% accuracy versus GPT-5 at 55.9%, rising to 70.1% when GPT-5 is paired with the Qwen3-Embedding-8B retriever.
methodology: Introduces BrowseComp-Plus, a fixed corpus derived from BrowseComp with human-verified supporting documents and mined hard negatives, enabling controlled disentanglement of agent vs. retriever contributions.
why_it_matters: Gives a concrete, reproducible retrieval-baseline ceiling (BM25 vs. dense retriever) that any claimed agentic gain must be measured against, and shows retriever choice alone swings accuracy by over an order of magnitude — directly anchors decision 1.
limitations: Corpus assembled per-query from the benchmark's own documents, later shown to bias evidence selection (see dc6612fba47a)
single benchmark family (BrowseComp)
relevance_reason: Directly measures the single-query retrieval baseline ceiling with a controlled corpus and disentangles retriever from agent contribution — the anchor paper for decision 1.

key_finding: Structured field extraction in HySemRAG achieves 35.1% higher semantic similarity than PDF chunking (0.655 vs 0.485, p<0.000001), with an agentic QA loop reaching 68.3% single-pass success and 99.0% citation accuracy.
methodology: Eight-stage pipeline combining hybrid retrieval (semantic search, keyword filtering, knowledge-graph traversal), agentic self-correction, and citation verification; evaluated across 643 observations from 60 testing sessions, applied to geospatial epidemiology literature.
why_it_matters: A concrete instance of the exact system class the brief targets — hybrid retrieval plus graph traversal plus agentic QA for literature synthesis — with citation-accuracy and extraction-quality numbers that could inform retrieval-architecture choices.
limitations: Single-author work with a small evaluation set and no comparison to a single-query baseline or existing agentic literature-search systems
applied to one epidemiology use case; generalization untested
relevance_reason: Directly instantiates a hybrid-retrieval, graph-traversal, agentic-QA system for literature synthesis matching the brief's system-design scope, though evaluation rigor is limited.

key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy distinguishing static vs. dynamic agent workflows and single- vs. multi-agent architectures, and critiques current benchmarks for restricted external-knowledge access, sequential inefficiencies, and metric misalignment with practical objectives.
methodology: Systematic survey/roadmap analyzing information acquisition strategies (API vs. browser), tool-use frameworks, and existing benchmarks for Deep Research agents; maintains a curated public repository.
why_it_matters: Gives the field's current taxonomy and names specific benchmark weaknesses (metric misalignment, restricted knowledge access) that decisions 3 and 4 need to be checked against before trusting any single system's reported numbers.
limitations: Survey, not new empirical evidence
benchmark critique is qualitative, not quantified
relevance_reason: Orienting survey that frames the taxonomy of agentic mechanisms and names benchmark construction weaknesses relevant to decisions 2-4.

key_finding: Introduces DeepResearch Bench, 100 PhD-level research tasks across 22 fields, with a reference-based adaptive-criteria report-quality metric and a citation-accuracy/effective-citation-count framework aligned with human judgment.
methodology: Expert-crafted task construction across 22 domains plus two novel evaluation methodologies (report quality, citation accuracy/coverage) validated against human judgment; framework open-sourced.
why_it_matters: A carefully constructed, expert-labeled benchmark with explicit citation-accuracy scoring gives a template for how literature-search-agent evaluation sets should be built (decision 3), separate from end-to-end report quality.
limitations: Tasks are general PhD-level research questions rather than literature-search-specific queries
abstract gives no explicit contamination controls
relevance_reason: A detailed account of benchmark construction methodology (task sourcing, expert labeling, citation-accuracy evaluation) directly relevant to decision 3.

key_finding: Relocating BrowseComp-Plus questions onto an independently built corpus (ClimbMix) causes the strongest agent's evidence recall to fall from 84.3% to 21.4% and answer accuracy to drop by five points, while search calls rise by 63%.
methodology: A projection pipeline decomposes each question into atomic reasoning hops and grounds every hop in a 400B-token, 553M-document corpus built without reference to any benchmark, verified by automatic checks, an independent agent, and human review; yields 57 fully grounded questions from 830 BrowseComp-Plus test questions.
why_it_matters: Directly shows that a benchmark's per-query corpus construction (documents selected per query, as in BrowseComp-Plus) inflates reported retrieval performance — exactly the decision-4 evidence the brief wants, that a reported gain does not survive a different, independently built corpus.
limitations: Very small resulting benchmark (57 questions) after strict verification
pipeline validated on only one source benchmark (BrowseComp-Plus) so far
relevance_reason: Directly demonstrates a reported agentic/retrieval gain shrinking dramatically under an independently constructed corpus, exactly the replication-failure evidence decision 4 asks for.

key_finding: Adding the Retrieval-Aware Agent Controller (RAAC) to deep research agents on BrowseComp-Plus reduces search calls by an average of 14 and improves the best-performing agent's accuracy by up to 10% (3% on average).
methodology: Analyzes reasoning trajectories of multiple deep-research agents to show most iterations add little value ('reasoning stagnation'), then introduces unsupervised signals (search novelty, information coverage) driving RAAC's action selection, evaluated across a large set of DRAs on BrowseComp-Plus.
why_it_matters: Isolates a specific controllable mechanism (novelty/coverage-aware stopping and action selection) as the source of measured gain, exactly the kind of mechanism attribution decision 2 needs rather than crediting the whole system.
limitations: Gains concentrated in the best-performing agent (10%) vs. average (3%), so benefit is agent-dependent
evaluated on one benchmark family (BrowseComp-Plus)
relevance_reason: Attributes a quantified performance gain to a specific, well-defined agentic control mechanism (retrieval-aware stopping/action selection), directly answering decision 2.

key_finding: EviReform's evidence-guided residual queries improve multi-hop graph retrieval by up to 5.59 Recall@5 points and 4.50 F1 points over the strongest baseline on 2WikiMultiHopQA, HotpotQA, and MuSiQue.
methodology: Separates residual-query formulation (from retrieved passages) from graph-based evidence aggregation, normalizing and combining original and residual retrieval signals propagated along entity-shared propositions; evaluated on three multi-hop QA benchmarks.
why_it_matters: Provides a concrete, quantified mechanism for combining query reformulation with graph traversal — the two specific agentic moves the brief names — clarifying which part of a hybrid design actually carries a measured retrieval gain.
limitations: Evaluated on generic multi-hop QA benchmarks rather than scientific literature/citation graphs
no comparison against a single-query database search baseline
relevance_reason: A quantified method paper isolating query reformulation combined with graph retrieval as the source of retrieval gain, directly informing decision 2 and the underlying retrieval-method question.

key_finding: DynaKRAG's learned state-conditioned policy for coordinating iterative retrieval, query reformulation, and sufficiency checking ranks first in EM/F1 across all nine dataset-backbone pairs, with 10.1-34.3% token efficiency and 15.1-43.4% retrieval-call efficiency gains.
methodology: Unified evidence-action framework with a deterministic validity layer, a learned continuation gate, and a learned advantage scorer over evidence operations; evaluated on HotpotQA, 2Wiki, and MuSiQue with three backbones (Qwen2.5-7B, GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.1-8B).
why_it_matters: Demonstrates that coordinating specific agentic operations (iterative retrieval, reformulation, sufficiency checking) via a learned policy, rather than a fixed pipeline, yields measurable efficiency and accuracy gains, informing how to attribute and design agentic mechanisms (decision 2).
limitations: Evaluated on generic multi-hop QA rather than scientific literature search
requires training a learned policy, adding complexity relative to prompted agent baselines
relevance_reason: Quantifies specific agentic evidence-control operations' contribution to retrieval gain and efficiency, directly relevant to decision 2's mechanism attribution question.

key_finding: PaperPilot's workflow-induction agent improves multi-turn scientific literature search over a base toolset agent, raising Hit@5 from 58.0 to 77.0, MRR from 47.5 to 59.4, nDCG@10 from 26.8 to 32.5, and cutting workflow execution errors from 9.5% to 0%.
methodology: Frames scientific literature search as induction of an executable DAG of operators (keyword search, citation expansion, filtering, scoring, reranking, evidence extraction); trained via supervised workflow imitation and preference optimization over controlled workflow corruptions, evaluated against a Qwen3.5-9B toolset-agent baseline.
why_it_matters: The most directly on-target system in the shortlist: an explicit, editable agentic workflow for scientific literature search combining citation expansion, reranking, and query refinement, with quantified gains over a fixed-pipeline agent — exactly the design comparison decision 2 needs.
limitations: Baseline is a toolset agent, not a plain single-query database search, so the decision-1 recall ceiling is not directly established
gains measured on the authors' own workflow-corruption training setup; generalization to independent benchmarks untested
relevance_reason: Directly matches the brief's system: a scientific-literature-search agent combining citation expansion, reranking, and query reformulation with quantified, decomposable gains over a fixed baseline.

key_finding: Across 26 full-text-coded autonomous research/AI-scientist systems, 83% release code but only 38% release seeds/execution traces or report any novelty-verification method, and no closed-loop system demonstrates an externally validated in-loop oracle.
methodology: Survey screening 125 candidate works, full-text coding 26 entries (24 runnable systems, two study/position papers) across seven audit dimensions (lifecycle stage, autonomy, evaluation, artifacts, human-in-the-loop, novelty verification, result-selection disclosure).
why_it_matters: Documents a broad reproducibility/verification gap in end-to-end AI-scientist systems, of which literature search is only one lifecycle stage — useful context for skepticism toward self-reported agentic gains generally, but it does not address retrieval baselines, benchmark construction, or mechanism attribution for search agents specifically.
limitations: Literature search is only one of many lifecycle stages covered; the survey does not isolate search-specific findings
qualitative audit coding rather than quantitative benchmark comparison
relevance_reason: Adjacent survey on reproducibility/verification gaps in AI-scientist systems broadly; touches decision 4's skepticism theme but is not focused on literature-search retrieval or benchmarks specifically.

key_finding: Search-Time Contamination — where deep research agents retrieve benchmark metadata, question context, or ground-truth answers via web search during evaluation — is widespread across six public benchmarks and inflates measured performance by up to 4%.
methodology: Defines three contamination severity levels (metadata leakage, question-context leakage, explicit answer leakage), builds detection algorithms, and evaluates modern deep research agents on six public benchmarks.
why_it_matters: Directly undermines the premise that reported agentic gains are real: some of the measured improvement on public benchmarks is search-time leakage rather than genuine reasoning or retrieval capability, meaning any comparison to single-query baselines run on the same contaminated benchmarks needs re-checking before its gain is trusted.
limitations: Benchmarks studied are general reasoning/QA benchmarks for deep research agents, not necessarily scientific-literature-search-specific sets
Contamination severity may vary by benchmark and agent architecture not covered here
relevance_reason: Directly answers the brief's question of where reported agentic gains fail to hold up, showing a concrete, measured mechanism (search-time leakage) that inflates benchmark scores.

key_finding: In Agentic GraphRAG, cited evidence is often necessary (removing it substantially changes answers) but not sufficient, since accurate answers also depend on uncited traversal context and surrounding graph structure.
methodology: Controlled ablation experiments isolating, removing, and masking cited and uncited graph entities during agentic knowledge-graph traversal; abstract gives no benchmark, dataset, or scale details.
why_it_matters: Suggests that evaluating an agentic literature-search system's citations alone (e.g. which papers it cites) can misjudge its actual reasoning, since uncited nodes visited during graph traversal may still be doing real work — a caution for how any citation-graph-traversal mechanism gets measured and credited.
limitations: Setting is generic knowledge-graph QA, not scientific-literature citation graphs or literature-search benchmarks
No baseline recall or agentic-gain measurement, only citation faithfulness analysis
Abstract gives no quantitative effect sizes
relevance_reason: Closely related work on graph-traversal provenance and citation faithfulness in agentic RAG, relevant to how citation-graph traversal as a mechanism should be evaluated, but studied outside the literature-search setting itself.
